paras: The attempted lynching of Charles Madder was an attack by a mob of several hundred people on the jail at Tiffin, Ohio, early on November 7, 1881, in an effort to seize Madder, a Heidelberg College divinity student held on the charge of shooting Phoebe Bernard. The sheriff's armed posse drove the crowd off after a fight in which officers were injured, and Madder was moved secretly to Fremont and then to the Toledo jail. The repulse was carried by wire across the country, while a Tiffin dispatch in the paper of Madder's home county called the reports false.

Madder, a student for the ministry from East Greenville in Stark County, was accused of shooting Miss Phoebe Bernard on a Tiffin street on the night of Thursday, November 3, after she again refused to renew a broken engagement. He hid overnight in a lumber yard while citizens searched for him, gave himself up the next day, and was hurried to jail, in the Perrysburg Journal's words, "to prevent his being lynched by an infuriated people." His friends said he was insane, and a brother said he had suffered from a disease of the brain. At a preliminary examination on November 5, held inside the jail because the authorities feared a lynching, he was bound over for first-degree murder.

At 1:30 on Monday morning, according to a Tiffin special to the Cincinnati Times-Star, a mob of several hundred appeared at the jail and demanded the keys. The sheriff, who had gathered an armed posse in advance, refused, and in the riot that followed officers named as Brick, Brist or Brisk and Lambertson were severely injured before the mob was repelled. A later news summary named the sheriff as Lease, said three officers were wounded when police tried to arrest Andy Moore, whom it called the mob's leader, and reported that Dennis Hallahan was captured with a rope.

Warrants were issued for the leaders, another attack was expected, and Captain Lepper's militia was ordered out. A Tiffin dispatch of November 8 said the streets stayed thronged that night, and that shortly before midnight Madder was taken out of the jail, after which the sheriff told the crowd it could attack the jail if it wished. He was driven to Fremont and on the morning of November 8 reached the county jail at Toledo in the charge of Policeman Cordon of Tiffin.

In Toledo Madder was kept from public view, and his brother was refused permission to see him. Beyond the warrants and Hallahan's capture, no report of a prosecution of the mob or of Madder's trial was found.

The Times-Star special first appeared in the Memphis Public Ledger on November 7 and ran the next day from Augusta, Maine, to Chicago and Wheeling, under headlines such as "Attempt at Lynching," "Application Before Judge Lynch" and, in the Somerset Herald on November 16, "Lynchers Routed." A shorter wire headed "Mob Repulsed" ran in Yankton and Los Angeles, and a condensed version in the Huntsville Gazette. The Public Ledger filed the story under "Ohio Pleasantries," the Memphis Daily Appeal had headed the shooting "A Rope Would Cure Him," and wire copy called Madder "the murderer" though he had only been bound over.

Ohio weeklies credited the "herculean efforts of the whole police force" (Perrysburg Journal) and described "indignant citizens" (Somerset Press), and the Wheeling Intelligencer praised the "Ingenuity of a Sheriff." The Stark County Democrat of Canton, in Madder's home county, printed a Tiffin dispatch calling the lynching reports "all false" and Tiffin people "peaceable," while its own local note said the hearing had been held in the jail for fear of a lynching. No report stated the race of Madder, Bernard or the mob.

The Democrat's dispatch is the only account denying an attempt; the Times-Star and National Associated Press specials, the Perrysburg Journal and the Toledo reports all describe one. The crowd was put at several hundred or about two hundred, and the injured at two named officers, three officers or "several" police. The Democrat's dispatch dated November 7 says Madder went to Fremont "last night," while the November 8 dispatches place his removal shortly before midnight that day.

accounts.label: Cincinnati Times-Star special (wire)
accounts.gist: At 1:30 a.m. several hundred demanded the keys; the sheriff's armed posse refused, a riot followed, two officers were severely injured, the mob was repelled; warrants issued and militia ordered out.

accounts.label: National Associated Press
accounts.gist: The mob attacked the jail to lynch Madder; two officers were severely wounded; the next night, with streets thronged, the prisoner was disguised and taken to Toledo and the sheriff told the crowd it could raid the jail.

accounts.label: Perrysburg Journal (Ohio weekly)
accounts.gist: On Sunday night several hundred citizens gathered to lynch Madder and were stopped only by the whole police force, several of whom were severely injured; the sheriff took the prisoner by carriage to Fremont and then Toledo.

accounts.label: Weekly news summary
accounts.gist: Sheriff Lease, forewarned, prepared; three officers were wounded trying to arrest mob leader Andy Moore; Dennis Hallahan was captured with a rope; sixty men guarded the jail the next evening.

accounts.label: Tiffin dispatch in Madder's home-county paper
accounts.gist: Reports of a lynching attempt were sensational and false; Tiffin people were peaceable and disposed to let the law take its course.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Times-Star special or a short wire under headlines such as 'Attempt at Lynching', 'Mob Repulsed', 'Lynchers Routed', calling Madder 'the murderer'.
Chicago Tribune headed it 'Application Before Judge Lynch' and the Memphis Public Ledger put it under 'Ohio Pleasantries'; the Memphis Daily Appeal headed the shooting 'A Rope Would Cure Him'.
Ohio weeklies credited the police and sheriff ('herculean efforts', 'indignant citizens'); the Wheeling Intelligencer praised the 'Ingenuity of a Sheriff'.
The Stark County Democrat's Tiffin dispatch denied any attempt and called the town peaceable, while its own local note said the hearing was held in jail for fear of lynching.
